To enact regulations. See Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 44, concerning another city in which three men, Reuven, Shimon, and Levi, were selected to act as brokers in the wine trade pursuant to a governmental order requiring each city to appoint brokers through the local authorities and under oath that they would act without fraud. The brokers were also required to maintain a protocol recording the number of barrels sold, and their brokerage fees were to be divided equally, even where a merchant dealt with only one broker and that broker personally went to the cellar. Reuven later claimed 150 gold coins as his share from the vintage season, which the others had withheld on the ground that they themselves had handled the transactions. Reuven argued that they were taking the share to which he was entitled under dina de-malchuta dina, while Shimon replied that most towns had not accepted this ordinance. Chatam Sofer discusses at length the scope of dina de-malchuta dina and the views of the Rishonim. He concludes that the governmental regulation limiting brokerage to appointed brokers does not conflict with Torah law. On the contrary, if the matter came before a beit din, it would be proper to establish a similar regulation so that the number of brokers not exceed what the city and its commerce can support, thereby allowing each to earn a livelihood without destroying the livelihood of another. This is common practice in many lands, where the number of craftsmen in each trade is regulated, and all the more so with brokers. A similar concept appears in Bava Batra regarding the butchers, and in Choshen Mishpat at the end of siman 231 concerning trade regulations intended to prevent one from cutting off another's livelihood. Maharik, cited also by Maharashdam, siman 407, writes that although in strict law any person subject to the taxes of the kingdom may trade in the city, if the townspeople see that outsiders are seriously damaging their livelihood they may petition the ruler to restrict them, even beyond the strict rule of law. Certainly that applies here. The further regulation that all brokerage fees be divided equally is likewise valid. With the butchers in Bava Batra and the bakers in the Tosefta, Torah law does not otherwise require one to work on one day while another must sit idle, yet once they associate on common terms they may enforce their arrangement with the approval of the communal authority. Dina de-malchuta is at least as strong for this purpose. Likewise, a rule that all craftsmen act as partners and that all profit fall into a common fund has an analogue in Torah law: regarding the priestly watch, all kohanim fit to serve in that watch share in the portions, and David HaMelech enacted that the share of one who goes down to battle is like the share of one who remains with the baggage. Here, moreover, Shimon and Levi themselves accepted Reuven into their partnership on this condition. According to one opinion in Rama, siman 176 seif 3, no formal kinyan is required, and where the law of the kingdom also governs, all agree that no kinyan is required. It is therefore clear that Shimon and Levi must give Reuven his share of what they already earned and of future earnings, so long as he has not been disqualified by the community and its judges.

Of all the townspeople. Baer Heitev cites the view that the Sema did not rule this way in the name of Rabbi Moshe Alashkar, siman 49. Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, end of siman 117, writes that Rabbi Moshe Alashkar's position is also that of Rivash, siman 399, namely that members of a particular trade require the consent of the communal scholar, whereas the townspeople as a whole do not. Rivash himself anticipated the Shach's objection and answered it. Chatam Sofer appears to rule like Rivash and Rabbi Moshe Alashkar, and in siman 116 he likewise writes that although the Shach disagrees, the Shach's objection can readily be rejected. However, Chut HaMeshulash, responsum 15 at the end of Tashbetz, cites Rivash and disagrees, adducing Rashba to show expressly that even the townspeople may not enact a regulation, where a Torah scholar is appointed over the community, without his consent. VeShav HaKohen, siman 92, likewise challenges Rivash and Rabbi Moshe Alashkar. He notes that their attribution to Rambam and Ramban is not established from Rambam, while Ramban's novellae indicate the opposite; Rashba, responsum 1206, also writes in Ramban's name that the townspeople may not regulate without the local sage. Rav Hai Gaon in Mishpetei Shevuot states the same, as do many Rishonim. VeShav HaKohen concludes that since Rav Hai Gaon, Ramban, Rashba, Semag, Rosh, Tur, Mordechai, Hagahot Maimoniyot in the names of Raavan and Rabbi Baruch, all make no distinction between craftsmen and townspeople, Rambam should also be understood that way. Thus Rama and Levush, who speak also of all the townspeople, are correct in halachah and practice. Baer Heitev further writes that even according to the view that a majority can compel the minority, this applies only when all were present for the deliberation. Beit Yosef, siman 13, cites Rashba that one follows the majority only when the majority emerged from the discussion of the entire body. A majority is legally significant only when it arises from the whole and from deliberation with the whole; otherwise, or when some were absent, the act is ineffective. Beit Yosef in Yoreh Deah, siman 228, similarly cites Rashba regarding a communal tax agreement: the agreement follows what all agreed upon, not what only some agreed upon, and even where the majority controls, that majority must have been formed in the presence of all, like ordinary adjudication. Get Pashut, in his general rules, rule 1, discusses this at length. Kenesset HaGedolah, siman 13, records several distinctions. If the first deliberation did not occur together, even if all later reconvene, the first group that already resolved the matter is considered interested in maintaining its original position, because it is embarrassing to retract and admit that the others corrected its error. Therefore its later numerical majority does not establish a valid majority. This is explained by Maharit, Choshen Mishpat, siman 79, and by other authorities. Maharit writes that even Mahari Beirav agrees to this; his disagreement in the controversy over semichah in Tzfat concerned a matter that required no adjudicatory inquiry, only communal selection of one sage for semichah according to Rambam. Mahara di Boton, however, understood Mahari Beirav as disagreeing with Ralnach. Birkei Yosef concludes that Maharit's reading is primary. Where all subsequently agree, Kehunat Olam records a dispute among later authorities. Maharashdam, Choshen Mishpat, siman 406, was asked about a community that normally assessed taxes every three years but made an early assessment against one individual while he was absent and greatly increased his assessment. He ruled that an ordinary individual could not object and the communal enactment stood, but if the absent person was one of the appointed officers or communal leaders, he could object, because Rashba requires a majority emerging from the whole. Birkei Yosef notes that Masa Melech challenged this as inconsistent with Maharashdam, siman 398, where a man who had been excluded from the synagogue was later assessed while absent, and Maharashdam ruled in his favor because all taxpayers normally participated in the assessment and he had not been summoned. He could say that had he been present he might have persuaded them to select different assessors. Penei Moshe reconciles the two responsa by distinguishing an individual who was in town but was not summoned, in which case he may object, from one who was out of town, in which case the required majority is the majority of those present, unless he is a communal officer whose absence always prevents action. Birkei Yosef prefers another reconciliation: the rule requiring a majority from the whole applies to a defined body of officers and leaders. In siman 406 the absent person was only an ordinary resident, so he was bound by the leaders' decision, while in siman 398 that community's custom was for all taxpayers to constitute the deliberative body. Thus every taxpayer there had the status of an appointed member, and omission of one was like omission of a communal officer elsewhere. See also what was written above, siman 163 seif 1.
To make enactments. See Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 44, concerning a city where three men, Reuven, Shimon, and Levi, were selected as brokers for wine sales pursuant to a governmental regulation that every city appoint brokers by official authorization and oath so that there should be no fraud. The regulation further required the brokers to maintain a protocol recording how many barrels were sold, and that brokerage fees be divided equally among them, even where a merchant dealt with only one broker and that broker personally went to the cellar. Reuven later claimed approximately one hundred fifty gold coins from the vintage season because Shimon and Levi had not given him his share, arguing that they themselves had transacted the business and had seized the portion to which he was entitled under the law of the kingdom. Shimon replied that most towns had never accepted this regulation. Chatam Sofer discusses at length the principle of dina d'malchuta dina and the early authorities, and concludes that the governmental regulation requiring officially selected brokers does not conflict with Torah law. On the contrary, if the matter came before a Jewish court, the court would likewise enact that the number of brokers not exceed what the size of the city and its commerce can sustain, so that each can earn a livelihood and they do not destroy one another's livelihood. This is also the practice throughout the countries, where numbers are fixed for various trades. All the more so with brokers, such regulation is found in many large towns. There is a parallel in the first chapter of Bava Batra regarding the butchers, and in Choshen Mishpat at the end of siman 231, and likewise communal enactments intended to prevent one person from cutting off another's livelihood. Maharik, cited also by Rashdam, siman 407, writes that although by strict law anyone subject to the tax of the kingdom cannot be barred by a city from conducting commerce there, if the townspeople see that outsiders are greatly destroying their livelihood they may seek governmental assistance to restrict them even though strict law would not otherwise provide that result. See what I wrote above, siman 156, seif 7, seif katan 17. All the more so here. The regulation that all brokerage fees be divided equally is also proper. Regarding the butchers in Bava Batra and the bakers in the Tosefta, we find no exact Torah precedent for one worker being forced to work on his assigned day while another sits idle and risks hunger. Nevertheless, once they join together, they may impose such arrangements with the approval of the communal scholar. The law of the kingdom is at least as strong for this purpose. Certainly they may establish that all craftsmen function as partners and all profit goes into a common fund. A parallel exists in Torah law, where regarding the priestly service the verse states, "the priest who offers it, it shall be his," yet Chazal received that this means every priest qualified to serve in that watch shares. King David likewise enacted that the share of one who goes down to battle equals the share of one who remains with the baggage. In the present case, moreover, Shimon and Levi themselves accepted Reuven among them on this condition. According to one view in Rama, siman 176, seif 3, even a formal kinyan is unnecessary, and here the governmental rule also applies, concerning which all agree no kinyan is required. It is therefore clear that Shimon and Levi must give Reuven his share of what they already earned and of what they will earn so long as he is not disqualified by the community and judges. See there:
We were all together. The tongue of clothing and corks that were all together and were fixed by the majority, but called:
Of all the townspeople. See Baer Heitev through his discussion of Sema, who does not write as Maharam Alshakar, siman 49, and the assertion that Maharam Alshakar's view is compelled. See Responsa Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, at the end of siman 117, who writes that Responsa Rivash, siman 399, says the same as Maharam Alshakar, and Kesef Mishneh cites it: specifically members of a trade require the consent of the city's scholar, but the townspeople as a whole do not. Rivash himself already anticipated Shach's objection and answered it well. Chatam Sofer appears to rule like Rivash and Maharam Alshakar. At the end of siman 116 he likewise writes that although Shach disagrees, his objection can readily be answered. However, in Responsa Chut HaMeshulash appended to Tashbetz, question 15, I saw the words of Rivash cited and rejected. He brings a responsum of Rashba explicitly ruling otherwise, namely that even the townspeople cannot make an enactment where there is a Torah scholar appointed over the community unless that scholar agrees. See there. Responsa VeShav HaKohen, siman 92, likewise discusses the matter at length and questions Rivash and Maharam Alshakar. Their attribution to Rambam and Ramban is unconvincing: Rambam proves nothing, while Ramban in his novellae appears explicitly to hold the opposite. Responsa Rashba, siman 1206, likewise cites Ramban as holding that even townspeople cannot enact regulations without the city's scholar. He also cites Rav Hai Gaon in Mishpetei Shevuot, gate 60, who rules likewise, and shows that many early authorities agree. He concludes that since Rav Hai Gaon, Ramban, Rashba, Semag, Rosh, Tur, Mordechai, Hagahot Maimoniyot in the name of Raavan, and Rabbi Baruch all hold that there is no distinction between members of a craft and the townspeople, we should certainly understand Rambam the same way. Otherwise, how could none of these authorities have noted Rambam as disagreeing? It is therefore beyond doubt that this is the practical halachah, and the wording of Rama and Levush, "or all the townspeople," is clear and correct in practice. See there. Baer Heitev further writes that even according to the view that the majority can compel the minority, this is only when everyone was present, and similarly that majority rule over the minority applies only when all were present at one meeting. This is explicit in Beit Yosef above, siman 13, citing Responsa Rashba, who writes that we follow a majority only where the majority emerged from discussion among all. A majority everywhere means a majority arising from the entire body after discussion with the entire body. Otherwise, or in the absence of some, their action has no effect. Beit Yosef in Yoreh Deah, siman 228, likewise cites Responsa Rashba, part 3, siman 304, concerning a communal agreement about taxation, that the agreement follows what all agreed upon and not what only some agreed upon. Even where majority rule applies, the majority's agreement is effective only if reached in the presence of all, like ordinary judicial decisions. See there. See Get Pashut at the end, general rule 1, on this subject. See also Knesset HaGedolah, siman 13, for several distinctions. In Hagahot Beit Yosef, letter 24, he writes that if the discussion was not held together, then even if afterward all reconvene and discuss the matter, while those who originally agreed outside the others' presence still maintain their earlier view, their majority does not establish a valid decision. They are interested parties, because they are embarrassed to retract and appear to have been corrected by the others, and will seek every argument to preserve their first position. This is clear from Maharit, Choshen Mishpat, siman 79. See what I wrote above, siman 17, seif 5, seif katan 10, and siman 33, seif 2, seif katan 5. Ralbach, in the ruling concerning semichah, page 278, column 4, Mishpetei Shmuel, siman 32, Mishpat Tzedek, part 2, siman 4, and Mahara Sasson, siman 71, all write similarly. Maharit, siman 79, writes that even Mahari Beirav agrees with this. He disagreed only in his particular case, concerning the semichah in which the rabbis of Tzefat agreed to ordain one sage according to Rambam, because that matter was not a halachic ruling requiring discussion and investigation but merely a collective choice of whom to ordain. Mahara Di Boton, in manuscript responsum siman 84, however, writes that Mahari Beirav disagreed with Ralbach. Birkei Yosef there, letter 5, writes that Maharit is the principal view and that Mahari Beirav himself clearly agrees, as appears from his responsa. Where all later agree, however, Responsa Kehunat Olam, at the end of siman 12, says this remains a dispute among later authorities. See what I wrote above, siman 163, seif 1, seif katan 1. See Responsa Rashdam, Choshen Mishpat, siman 406, concerning a community whose custom was to make a tax assessment every three years. On one occasion they assessed an individual early, substantially increasing his assessment while he was absent from the city, and he later objected. Rashdam ruled that the individual cannot protest and the communal action stands, unless the objecting person was one of the appointed officials or community leaders. In that case he could object, based on Rashba's rule that the majority must emerge from all and that what the community did without one of its appointed members is ineffective. But if he was merely an ordinary individual, the community's act binds him. Birkei Yosef above, siman 13, letter 7, cites Masa Melech as questioning this because Rashdam himself appears to rule otherwise in siman 398. There Reuven had been opposed by many members of his community, who barred him from entering the synagogue, and they later wished to assess him for taxes. He argued, "What do I have to do with you, when you have rejected me?" Rashdam ruled in Reuven's favor and wrote, among other reasons, that Reuven was one of the taxpayers and all taxpayers had gathered to make the assessment, but he had not been summoned. He could say that had he been present, the assessors selected might have been different because he could have advanced reasons everyone would accept. Rashdam cites the principle that majority means a majority drawn from all, as taught by the Rosh, Rashba, and Ralbach. Thus in siman 398 he relied on that rule for a single absent individual, while in siman 406 he limited it to an official or community leader. Responsa Pnei Moshe, part 2, siman 110, reconciles the two by saying that even an ordinary individual may object when an act was done in his absence because there was no majority drawn from all, but this applies only where the person was in the city and was not invited, as in siman 398. If he was outside the city, majority is measured from those present. Siman 406 concerns such an absent person, and therefore Rashdam distinguishes only an official or community leader, whose absence can still invalidate the act. Birkei Yosef does not find this reconciliation persuasive from the wording of Rashdam in siman 406. He instead suggests that Rashdam always understood the requirement of a majority drawn from all to apply only to selected representatives, such as officials and community leaders, which is the simple sense of siman 406 and also fits his rulings in Yoreh Deah, simanim 68 and 82. Therefore, in siman 406, if the objector is merely an ordinary individual, even if he was in the city, he must obey whatever the community leaders agreed. This assumes the common communal structure in which only heads of the community participate in such decisions. Siman 398, by contrast, concerned a community whose custom was that all taxpayers attend and are counted, as is explicit in Rashdam's words that "all gathered to make the assessment and he was not called." Since by local custom all taxpayers were members of the deciding body, every taxpayer was effectively an appointed participant. The absent man's position was therefore like that of an absent official elsewhere, and Rashdam ruled in his favor. See there, and see what I wrote further above, siman 163, seif 1, seif katan 1:

Or the approval of all residents of the city is effective, etc. The Rosh writes this in the chapter HaShutafin, adding that members of a trade are regarded as the residents of the city concerning matters of that trade. See there. It appears that he had to write this, and the ruling is both correct and compelled. The Gemara challenges Rava from the earlier teaching that residents of a city may establish prices, and answers that this applies only where no distinguished scholar is present. This proves that even the residents of the city may not enact such regulations without him. Moreover, if the residents of the city possessed greater authority than members of a trade, how could the Gemara challenge Rava from the case of city residents? I therefore rule as the Rama writes. The Sema does not write this, based upon Responsa Mahari Alashkar, and the Kesef Mishneh likewise differs, based upon the Rivash. In my opinion, however, the proof stated above is conclusive. I found this among writings from my youth. See Responsa Rabbi Shmuel Kohen associated with part 2, siman 9; Responsa Rabbi Yosef Beit Levi, siman 29; Responsa Rabbi Eliyahu Mizrachi; Responsa Mahari ibn Lev, part 1, pages 144 and 192, and further at the end of that volume; and part 4 of Mahari ibn Lev concerning parts 1 and 2.
